set_up.model: encoder-decoder LSTM: an encoder LSTM runs over a 365-day history of meteorological and basin-attribute inputs, a separate decoder LSTM runs over the 0-7 day forecast horizon with meteorological forecasts as input; hidden size 256 in both; the end state of the encoder is handed to the decoder through a linear transfer for the cell state and a tanh layer for the hidden state; 50,000 minibatches of 256; reported hydrograph = mean of 3 separately trained models, each taken as the median of its predicted distribution
set_up.loss: negative log-likelihood of an asymmetric Laplace distribution predicted at every time step and lead time (not a squared-error loss)
set_up.inputs_listed: ECMWF IFS HRES daily-aggregated forecasts (total precipitation, 2-m temperature, surface net solar radiation, surface net thermal radiation, snowfall, surface pressure); the same six variables from ERA5-Land; NOAA CPC gauge-based daily precipitation analysis; NASA IMERG Early Run precipitation; HydroATLAS basin attributes. All area-averaged over the basin upstream of each gauge. No streamflow is used as an input.
set_up.lead_times: 0 to 7 days; lead 0 = prediction for the current day (a 'nowcast')
set_up.data: 5,680 gauges, 152,259 gauge-years in total; evaluation 1984-2021 for the 0-day results, the captions of Extended Data Figs 8-9 state that the lead-time metrics are calculated on 2014-2021
set_up.validation: random 10-fold cross-validation over gauges combined with a split in time, so every score is out-of-sample in both space and time; extra splits by continent (k=6), climate zone (k=13) and groups of hydrologically separate basins (k=8) are reported only in Extended Data Figs 8-9
set_up.benchmark: GloFAS version 4; only its 0-day lead (nowcast) could be benchmarked because the reforecast archive of GloFAS v4 was incomplete; GloFAS was NOT tested out-of-sample (mix of gauged and ungauged sites, calibration and validation years), which the authors say favours GloFAS
set_up.event_definition: an event counts as correctly predicted if the modelled and the observed hydrograph each cross their own return-period threshold (US Bulletin 17b, separately for model and observations) within two days of each other

what_it_says: An LSTM that sees forecast weather (ECMWF HRES) for the coming days, and no river gauge reading, gives flood-event reliability at 1-year to 5-year return periods up to 5 days ahead that is the same as, or better than, GloFAS reliability for the current day.

At 0-day lead the share of gauges where the AI model is strictly better than GloFAS is 64%, 70%, 60% and 49% for 1-, 2-, 5- and 10-year events, and the share where it is at least as good is 65%, 73%, 73% and 76%, so for rarer events more gauges are a tie rather than a win.

The 5-year-event precision of the AI model is not different from GloFAS precision for 1-year events, and its 5-year recall is better, which is what the abstract summarises as 'accuracy over 5-year events similar to or better than today's over 1-year events'.

The model is one network for all gauges; during training, missing forecast-product data were filled from a similar variable of another source (for HRES, from ERA5-Land) or by a mean value plus a flag, which indicates that the archive of HRES forecasts did not cover the whole 1984-2021 training period.

The model reads its weather input as basin averages and no streamflow input; the authors give the lack of real-time gauge data in many places and the fact that GloFAS has no streamflow input as the reasons.

Skill depends on basin size and aridity: the AI model does better in smaller basins, and both systems do better in humid basins, as drainage area, PET, AET and elevation are the most important attributes in the random-forest skill predictor.
nearing2024.what_it_does_not_say: It does not run an ablation, so it does not say how much of the skill comes from the HRES forecast input as against the reanalysis and satellite inputs, and nothing about a model with versus without forecast input. The text does not state which of the four weather products feeds the encoder and which the decoder. It gives no NSE or KGE values in the text (they are in Extended Data Figs 8-9, images), no recall or F1 at 1-day lead alone, and no score for basins in the south-eastern United States. Its event metric (threshold crossing within +-2 days, thresholds taken from the model's own record) differs from a 'flood onset' warning rate, so its percentages cannot be set beside our 19% and 64%.

what_it_says: In a same-day simulation task on CAMELS, median NSE of an LSTM rises with every increase of the number of training basins that was tried, up to all 531, and the authors say that even 531 are probably not enough; they recommend using at least hundreds of basins, whatever the target basin.

Conceptual and process models calibrated on one basin beat the same models calibrated regionally, but for LSTMs it is the other way round (Fig. 3: one LSTM trained on all 531 basins against one LSTM per basin, ensembles of 10 in both cases).

Training on hydrologically similar groups (by hydrological unit or by attribute cluster) is better than a random group of the same size but worse than all 531 basins; every subset model is worse than the full model in more basins than it is better.

Mechanism offered for extreme events: with a linear output layer the largest flow an LSTM can predict is limited by its weights, and a model trained on many basins has a larger range, so a single-basin model cannot reach many test flows (more than 6,346 test-period flows lie above the limit of their single-basin models, against 10 for the regional model).

Appendix E: the gain from regional training shows in correlation-based metrics (NSE, KGE, Pearson r) and in the variance ratio (high flows), only slightly in the timing and capture of hydrograph peaks, and not in bias.
kratzert2024.what_it_does_not_say: The page text gives no numbers for Fig. 6; all NSE values above are read by eye from the plot and carry the uncertainty of that reading. The x-axis point at one basin is not described in the text. Training length (about 9 years) is fixed.

what_it_says: I found no analysis of skill against the number of training basins or the number of training years in this paper; the page contains no such figure or table.

The only statement on data amount is a remark in the discussion: neural networks need a lot of training data, the authors' unpublished results indicate that it is often difficult to train an LSTM reliably on one catchment even with decades of data, and the transfer of information from similar catchments is what makes the regional approach work.

Training with the basin-normalised NSE* loss instead of plain MSE did not change the median NSE significantly; it improved the weak basins (lower end of the NSE distribution) and cut the number of basins with NSE below zero, because low-flow basins carry little weight in an MSE loss.
Giving the all-basin LSTM static basin attributes raises its mean NSE by 0.30 (NSE* loss) to 0.44 (MSE loss).
kratzert2019.what_it_does_not_say: It does not report skill against the number of training basins or years, nothing on forecasts or lead times, and no peak-aimed loss; the NSE* loss it uses is normalised per basin, not weighted towards peaks. The initial forget-gate bias is still not read (as in the existing record).

what_it_says: GEFSv12's reforecast dataset is large and public: 31 years, 25-km model, daily 5-member runs (11 members on Wednesdays), 3-hourly precipitation at 0.25 degree for 10 days, free on AWS for 2000-2019.

For 24-h rainfall over the contiguous US the 11-member reforecast is skilful against climatology but not close to perfect: its Brier skill score falls from 0.576 (12-36 h) to 0.513 (60-84 h) for 1 mm and from 0.418 to 0.334 for 5 mm; the heavier the rain the lower the skill, and the reliability curves are close to the diagonal at low probabilities and veer away from it at high probabilities (the authors' description).
GEFSv12 is better than the older GEFS_SubX reforecast, mostly at leads shorter than about 10 days, for reliability the two are alike for 1 mm and GEFSv12 is slightly closer to the diagonal for 5 mm.

The authors state that, as expected, forecast-driven runs generally score lower than the reanalysis-driven runs even at short lead times, because IFS forecasts carry biases that ERA5 (which is nudged with observations) does not; the table shows large drops at some gauges (LABW4 0.922 to 0.685, ARWN8 0.635 to 0.025) and small ones at others (NFDC1 0.897 to 0.876, TRAC2 0.897 to 0.876).

The gauges where the LSTM and GloFAS struggle most are flashy ones whose main variability is diurnal, while slow, large-catchment gauges are well forecast; LSTM forecasts had similar KGE and higher NSE than persistence at most gauges.

The authors justify training on reanalysis rather than on archived forecasts by reproducibility and by the lack of a consistent multi-decade forecast archive for most users, and call the resulting evaluation conservative.

what_it_says: The authors state that a model trained on reanalysis and then run on operational forecasts loses skill (a 'domain shift', which they attribute to differences in the error structure of the forecasts) and that this limit is largely independent of architecture.

Fine-tuning the reanalysis-pre-trained LSTM on IFS 1-day forecasts left the median nearly unchanged (change in KGE' -0.013, in NSE -0.032) but strongly improved the poorly performing basins (mean KGE' 0.21 to 0.44); in an ablation the median KGE' of the two-stage model (0.663) was 0.018 above a model trained on IFS forecasts only (0.645) and 0.059 above a mixed one-stage model (0.604), a gain the authors credit to the many extra basins in the pre-training.

Fed with real IFS forecasts and no gauge input, the model's median skill falls quickly with lead time: KGE' from 0.66 (day 1) to 0.51 (day 3) to 0.21 (day 10) and NSE from 0.53 to about 0.19 at day 3 (by eye), negative after day 5, mostly because the correlation falls, not the bias or variance.
The model tends to underestimate peaks: its precision for events up to 5 years is high (0.85-1.00) with exact-day matching, which the authors read as conservative behaviour.
taccari2026.what_it_does_not_say: Global Caravan basins (1,035 test basins in North America), no river-gauge input, daily weather from IFS rather than GEFS, and no CAMELS-US or south-eastern result; the lead-time curve uses weights trained on lead-1 forecasts and a window in which the past days are also forecasts, so it understates what an operational set-up (observed past, forecast future, trained on archived forecasts of each lead) could reach and cannot be set beside a perfect-forecast ceiling. No recall for 1-day-ahead flood onsets.

set_up.data: SIMULATED data: 200 synthetic rainfall events generated by stochastic storm transposition over the Iowa River basin and run through the HEC-HMS hydrological model; the LSTM predicts the model's own hourly streamflow 1 to 12 h ahead; the training set is 40 of the events, the test set 9,600 samples
set_up.model: LSTM encoder-decoder; losses compared: MSE, pinball (quantile 0.8 and 0.9) and an 'asymmetric peak' loss = MSE plus an extra MSE term times F = 3.0 where the simulated flow exceeds T = 0.45 of the normalised range (155 m3/s) and the model under-predicts

numbers.quantity: overall NSE, MSE loss -> asymmetric peak loss, lead 1 h
NSE on flows above 155 m3/s, MSE -> asymmetric peak loss, lead 1 h
overall NSE, MSE -> asymmetric peak loss, lead 12 h
NSE on flows above 155 m3/s, MSE -> asymmetric peak loss, lead 12 h
pinball loss (quantile 0.9): overall NSE / NSE above 155 m3/s, lead 1 h; lead 12 h

what_it_says: In a synthetic single-basin setting a squared-error loss makes the LSTM under-predict the high flows (NSE above 155 m3/s as low as -0.90 at 12 h), and a loss that penalises under-prediction above a threshold more heavily lifted that peak-flow NSE to 0.62 at 12 h and 0.76 at 1 h, while also raising the overall NSE (0.88 to 0.96 at 12 h).
The pinball (quantile) loss helped peaks at the shortest lead times but not at 12 h, where the asymmetric peak loss was the better choice.
tofighi2025.what_it_does_not_say: The flows are the output of a hydrological model for synthetic storms in one basin, not gauge observations, with hourly steps and 1-12 h leads, so the size of the gain is an upper-bound type result that cannot be carried to daily observed flows in the south-eastern US; threshold and factor (T, F) were tuned on the same kind of data; no comparison with a peak-detection (onset) metric.
not_found: any real-gauge or CAMELS test of a peak-aimed loss in this paper

dahal2026.where_read: abstract on the Arizona State University repository page, read as text on 2026-10-07; the paper itself was not opened.

numbers.quantity: catchments (CAMELS via the Caravan framework) / loss functions combined / forecast horizon
numbers.value: 482 / 8 (MSE, NSE, KGE, Huber, quantile 0.15 and 0.85, expectile 0.15 and 0.85) / daily up to 30 days

numbers.quantity: coverage of the uncertainty band on unseen data, forecast of 1 / 7 / 30 days

what_it_says: LSTMs trained with eight different loss functions, among them quantile and expectile losses that put weight on the high or the low end, were combined by linear stacking; the abstract states that the ensemble beat each single-loss model in NSE significantly at all horizons.
dahal2026.what_it_does_not_say: The abstract gives no NSE values and no peak or flood metric, so the effect of any single peak-aimed loss on high flows is not stated; the forecasts of 1-3 days are not singled out.
not_found: per-loss NSE or peak metrics (abstract only)

not_verified: Hamill et al. 2013: ETS, correlation or reliability of 24-h precipitation at days 1-3 (the article body was not readable); only the abstract and the dataset's configuration were read.

Guan et al. 2022: no ETS and no correlation are reported there; only Brier skill score and reliability for two windows (12-36 h, 60-84 h) over the contiguous US on a 1 degree grid; nothing for the south-eastern US or for catchment-scale rain.
Kratzert et al. 2019b (WRR): the full text; number of folds and periods; any skill-versus-number-of-basins result in it.
Kratzert et al. 2019a (HESS): confirmed that the page has no skill-versus-number-of-basins or -years analysis; Tables 2 and 3 (images) were not re-read.
Kratzert et al. 2024: the Fig. 6 numbers are read by eye (about +-0.003); the exact values are in the authors' run directories on Zenodo (10.5281/zenodo.10139248), not opened.
Taccari et al. 2026 Fig. 8a: NSE at leads 2 to 5 is read by eye (about +-0.02); the paper is a preprint.
Nearing et al. 2024: no ablation of the HRES forecast input, no NSE/KGE values in the text, no 1-day-lead recall; Extended Data figures not read.
Hunt et al. 2022: Fig. 11 (NSE/KGE against lead) not read; the 5-day LSTM value for BNDN5 is blank in the table file; periods of the ERA5-driven test and the IFS-driven run differ.

No paper found in which an LSTM with a river-gauge input is trained on GEFS (or GEFS reforecast) precipitation on CAMELS and the gain at 1-3 days is reported against the same model without forecast input.

No paper found that adds satellite (SMAP, ESA CCI) or reanalysis soil moisture as an LSTM input for streamflow and reports the skill difference. Fang and Shen 2020 (soil-moisture forecasting with data integration) was not opened because it predicts soil moisture itself, not streamflow.

No real-gauge (CAMELS or similar) ablation of a peak-aimed loss with numbers at 1-3 days was found; the only quantified one (Tofighi et al. 2025) uses simulated hourly data in one basin. A claim seen in a search snippet that better extreme-event skill generally costs overall skill was not verified at a source.
Dahal et al. 2026 and Frame et al. 2021: abstract only; Soucy et al. 2025: conference abstract only; Sharma et al. 2021: arXiv preprint, journal version not checked.
